Multi-omics has shifted from a methodological aspiration to a routine design choice in the life sciences. Simultaneous profiling of genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic and microbial layers captures interactions that no single assay can resolve, and the conceptual rationale for combining these layers is no longer in dispute [R54]. What has lagged behind this conceptual maturation, however, is the software infrastructure that researchers must actually use. In our assessment of the field, a typical multi-omics project now involves roughly five to seven data types and on the order of several thousand samples, with each analytical step admitting a dozen or more competing implementations; these figures are author estimates rather than findings cited from the literature. The tooling has accumulated faster than the standards that should govern it, and the result is an analytical gap that is no longer conceptual but infrastructural: researchers spend more time reconciling file formats, harmonizing object classes and reproducing someone else's R environment than they do interpreting biological signal.

The heterogeneity of the available tools is striking. On the R side, Bioconductor provides the foundational data structures, most notably MultiAssayExperiment, which offers coordinated representation, storage and operation on diverse genomics datasets and ships with ready-to-analyze TCGA objects [R28]; on top of this substrate the community has built package-specific integrators such as mixOmics with its DIABLO supervised framework [R27], the longitudinal timeOmics [R20] and netOmics packages [R21], the vertical and horizontal miodin workflow [R48], the MOFA-based transfer-learning extension MOTL [R32], the MuSA radiogenomic GUI built on the same MultiAssayExperiment class [R25], and reproducibility-oriented wrappers such as moiraine that preprocess data, run one or more integration methods and enable head-to-head comparison across integration tools [R3]. The Python ecosystem is no less crowded, ranging from graph-neural-network frameworks such as BioNeuralNet [R5] to specialised deep-learning integrators including MOADLN, which uses self-attention and a Multi-Omics Correlation Discovery Network to combine omics-specific encoders before classification [R17], MCluster-VAEs [R22], MO-GCAN [R29], DeepMoIC [R12] and MoAGL-SA [R39]. Parallel to these programmatic ecosystems, web-based point-and-click platforms have proliferated: the Analyst suite (ExpressAnalyst, MetaboAnalyst, OmicsNet, OmicsAnalyst) [R8], ExpOmics [R41], the single-cell analyst [R6], CFViSA, a free web platform integrating 79 tools with microbiome and transcriptome pipelines [R40], NOODAI [R33], PhenoMultiOmics [R14] and disease-specific portals such as CPMOAD [R7] and LOSTdb [R34] now offer GUI-driven alternatives that lower the barrier to entry but introduce their own concerns about transparency and reproducibility. Finally, containerised, workflow-management approaches — Nextflow, Snakemake and WorkflowHub-compatible Research Object Crates [R11, R18, R26, R35] — attempt to capture provenance at the level of the analysis environment itself.

Among these application domains, host–microbiome research exemplifies the infrastructural pressure particularly acutely. Microbial community samples bring together metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, metaproteomics and metabolomics, with sample coverage that is intrinsically inconsistent across layers because taxa differ in their genomic recoverability, expression detectability and chemical extractability [R1, R54]. As the microbial multi-omics perspective of Van Den Bossche and colleagues emphasises, the complexity of analysing a single isolate is multiplied further when samples comprise hundreds to thousands of individual species, yet standardised workflows and benchmarked datasets remain scarce [R54]. This combination — heterogeneous data formats, inconsistent sample coverage, complex analytical chains and weak reproducibility standards — illustrates the kind of field-level bottleneck that workflow-level solutions such as EasyMultiProfiler (EMP) attempt to address. EMP is an R workflow built on SummarizedExperiment and MultiAssayExperiment that organises extraction, preparation, support, analysis and visualisation into a single coherent pipeline [R1]. Microbiome multi-omics is therefore not just another application area; it is a particularly demanding setting in which any claim that multi-omics infrastructure has matured is put to the test.

A candid assessment must temper the cataloguing instinct. The sheer number of tools is often taken as evidence of progress, yet the evidence reviewed here describes a field in which each new publication tends to add another integration method rather than consolidate best practice. Benchmarking studies of cancer subtype clustering [R4], multi-omics biomarker discovery [R50] and single-cell integration [R10, R37] consistently find that no single method dominates across datasets, and that gains over simpler baselines are often modest. The persistence of batch effects, platform-specific artefacts and the absence of agreed-upon reference datasets mean that methodological choice — not biological signal — frequently determines the headline result. Tool catalogues lengthen faster than standards mature, and the fragmentation that integration was meant to solve remains, in many respects, intact. The review that follows takes this tension as its starting point: it surveys the available software landscape across general-purpose frameworks, microbiome-centred tools, GUI platforms and containerised infrastructure, examines the limited but informative benchmarking evidence, and uses EasyMultiProfiler as a worked example of what a domain-specific, workflow-level solution can — and cannot — deliver relative to its alternatives.

A useful organizing principle for the heterogeneous landscape of multi-omics integration software is the point in the analytical pipeline at which information from different omics layers is allowed to interact. Three regimes are routinely distinguished in the methodological literature: early integration, in which raw or preprocessed features from each omics layer are concatenated into a single matrix and fed to one downstream learner; intermediate integration, in which each omics is first summarized in its own representation and the resulting views are then fused in a joint latent space, graph, or factor decomposition; and late integration, in which omics-specific models are trained independently and their outputs are combined only at the decision or prediction stage. This taxonomy, while inevitably simplified, maps cleanly onto the principal algorithmic families represented in the corpus reviewed here, and it provides a frame against which claims of methodological novelty can be assessed.

Early integration remains the most straightforward strategy and the easiest to implement on top of generic machine-learning toolkits. In its classical form it underlies pipelines that learn patient embeddings or disease classifiers directly from concatenated feature vectors. The contrastive adversarial encoder CAEncoder treats the integrated matrix as input to a Vision Transformer trained end-to-end against a CycleGAN-based adversarial objective [R30]. The appeal of this regime lies in its simplicity and in its compatibility with any supervised learner; its principal weaknesses, by contrast, are the curse of dimensionality when omics blocks differ in scale and the implicit assumption that cross-omics interactions can be captured by a single monolithic model.

Intermediate integration has become the dominant paradigm in bulk and single-cell multi-omics research. The most influential instances are joint matrix-factorization methods, similarity-based fusion algorithms, and conceptual frameworks that combine per-omics representations with downstream multi-omics analyses. The MOADLN framework uses self-attention to capture patient correlations and a Multi-Omics Correlation Discovery Network to learn cross-omic label correlations for biomedical data classification [R17]. The MOFA family and its transfer-learning extension MOTL exemplify the factor-analytic branch, projecting each omics into a shared low-dimensional space whose factors can be annotated biologically and used for downstream clustering or regression [R32]. Similarity network fusion and its descendants constitute a parallel branch that constructs per-omics patient graphs and iteratively fuses them into a single affinity matrix; in the recent benchmarking of eight representative early, intermediate and late integration methods on TCGA colorectal cancer data, SNF emerged as the strongest performer on both simulated and real-world datasets [R4]. Conceptual schemes such as STATegra formalize the intermediate regime by stepwise combining a per-omics machine-learning component analysis with a non-parametric data-combination step and multi-omics exploratory analysis [R24]. A more recent wave of intermediate methods adds deep representation learning to this template. DeepMoIC uses autoencoders to obtain compact per-omics embeddings and then incorporates a patient similarity network through a graph-convolutional architecture [R12]; MCluster-VAEs employs a unified variational autoencoder with an attention mechanism to learn cluster-friendly representations in an end-to-end fashion [R22]; MoAGL-SA generates patient graphs from each omics with graph learning and uses self-attention to weight per-omics graph embeddings adaptively before classification [R39]; MO-GCAN combines per-omics graph convolutional networks with a sample-fusion graph attention network for supervised subtyping across eight cancer types [R29]; and TMODINET adds a Dirichlet-based uncertainty estimation head to a self-attention and graph-convolutional backbone to address the trustworthiness of predictions in clinical settings [R9]. The supervised feature-selection framework DIABLO from the mixOmics package sits at the boundary of intermediate and supervised integration, since it constructs sparse latent components that are jointly predictive of phenotypic groups while remaining interpretable as correlated biomarker signatures; the same joint-decomposition philosophy underlies several of the survival-prediction benchmarks that combine per-omics regularized regressions at the score level [R27, R46].

Late integration, in which each omics produces its own prediction that is then aggregated, is conceptually the most modular and the least prone to dominance by the highest-variance view. Software-side support for late fusion is less conspicuous than for the other two regimes, but it is implicitly used whenever pipelines train separate per-omics classifiers or survival models and combine them at the score level, as in parts of the multi-omics biomarker benchmark that compared 20 statistical, machine-learning and deep-learning methods against gold-standard prognostic and therapeutic biomarkers across five cancer datasets [R50]. The reduced representation of each omics to a prediction score also makes late integration attractive when cohorts are partially overlapping and omics blocks differ in availability.

A second axis that cuts orthogonally across this pipeline taxonomy is the degree of supervision. Unsupervised methods dominate the discovery-oriented literature, where the goal is subtype identification, dimensionality reduction or biomarker prioritization without external labels; representative tools include SNF [R4], MOFA and MOTL [R32], MCluster-VAEs [R22] and the CancerSubtypes package that wraps four unsupervised subtype-discovery approaches with standardized preprocessing [R49]. Supervised methods, in turn, are preferred when gold-standard endpoints such as cancer subtype, drug response or survival are available; DIABLO [R27], MOADLN [R17], MO-GCAN [R29], TMODINET [R9] and the survival-prediction benchmark that evaluated 11 methods across 18 TCGA datasets all belong to this category [R46]. The systematic survival benchmark is notable because it reported that only one of the multi-omics methods, block forest, outperformed a clinical Cox model, providing one of the few head-to-head empirical demonstrations that more elaborate integration architectures do not always yield better predictions than simpler baselines [R46].

Single-cell multimodal integration adds a third dimension to this scheme because it must reconcile modalities measured on the same cell, on matched cells across modalities, or on different cells within a population. The benchmark of 14 protein-abundance prediction algorithms and 18 single-cell integration algorithms on 47 datasets found totalVI and scArches to be the top protein predictors and Seurat, MOJITOO and scAI to be the strongest vertical integrators [R10], while a parallel benchmark of 12 multi-omics integration methods on RNA and ATAC data emphasized that no single method dominates across the six evaluation aspects considered [R37]. Domain-specific tools such as scMGAT for joint RNA, protein, methylation and ATAC integration [R51] and ScSmOP for single-cell single-molecule multiomics data [R19] further populate this niche.

A critical reading of the literature reveals two persistent limitations of the proposed taxonomy. First, the same architectural template, most prominently the combination of graph attention networks with per-omics encoders, is re-instantiated with minor variations across cancers, omics combinations and prediction tasks [R12, R29, R39, R42, R51], and the accompanying papers typically demonstrate improvement over a small, often self-curated, baseline set rather than over state-of-the-art supervised or factor-analytic methods evaluated under matched conditions. Second, claims about the superiority of early, intermediate or late fusion are rarely supported by rigorous head-to-head evaluation: the CRC benchmark [R4], the survival benchmark [R46], the single-cell integration benchmarks [R10, R37] and the multi-omics biomarker benchmark [R50] all show that the relative ranking of integration strategies is dataset-dependent, and that simpler early or late approaches can be competitive with, or superior to, more elaborate intermediate models in specific settings. The taxonomy is therefore best used as a descriptive device rather than as evidence for any universal methodological hierarchy.

General-purpose integration frameworks can be grouped along a continuum from tools that genuinely abstract the integration step—exposing it as a swappable component in a wider workflow—to packages that hard-wire a single algorithm and treat preprocessing or visualization as the only configurable layer. The most useful abstractions decouple three concerns: the data container, the integration operator, and the downstream statistical or biological interpretation. The R/Bioconductor ecosystem has been particularly fertile for this style of design. The moiraine package builds reproducible multi-omics pipelines that preprocess heterogeneous omics layers, dispatch them to one or more user-chosen integration methods, and return standardized outputs so that results can be compared across algorithms [R3]. Similarly, miodin offers a workflow-based syntax in which the same pipeline language supports vertical integration (same samples profiled on different platforms) and horizontal integration (same variables measured across studies), enabling transparent re-use of the same analysis scaffolding across transcriptomics, genomics and proteomics [R48]. timeOmics extends this philosophy to temporal designs—providing preprocessing, modeling and clustering of longitudinal multi-omics data and demonstrating it on the integrative Human Microbiome Project diabetes dataset combining mRNA, metabolites, gut taxa and clinical variables [R20]—while its companion netOmics builds hybrid multi-omics networks with smart node labeling and propagation to extract interpretable relationships from the same kind of data [R21]. These four packages share the property that the integration algorithm is an explicit, named object in the workflow: the user is not buying a single method but a methodology-neutral execution engine.

A second tier of R packages is method-centric yet generalizable, exposing a single integrative operator but with rich preprocessing, validation and visualization surrounding it. mixOmics and its supervised DIABLO extension [R27] form the canonical example, with reproducible workflows demonstrated for plant multi-omics under abiotic stress combining phenomics, metabolomics, proteomics and transcriptomics [R16]. CancerSubtypes packages four established subtype-identification algorithms behind a common interface, allowing feature selection, validation and biological follow-up to be swapped in and out [R49]. MUUMI sits between these tiers: it is presented as a unified R framework for statistical meta-analysis coupled with similarity network fusion and molecular interactome inference, but its integration layer is essentially fixed—the value-add is the coupling of meta-analysis to network interpretation rather than algorithm interchangeability [R2]. FindIT2 occupies a more specialized niche, providing a complete framework for TF target inference from ChIP-seq/ATAC-seq and RNA-seq that is highly generalizable across species but constrained to a single biological question [R45]. The Python side is currently less populated by neutral abstraction layers and more by deep-learning frameworks with fixed graph architectures, exemplified by BioNeuralNet, a modular graph neural network framework for end-to-end network-based multi-omics analysis [R5].

The benchmarking literature tempers expectations about the relative merit of these approaches. A large-scale study of 11 survival prediction methods across 18 TCGA multi-omics datasets found that methods explicitly accounting for multi-omics group structure performed only marginally better than naive single-block baselines, and only the block-forest variant—a tree-based ensemble that respects block boundaries—meaningfully outperformed a clinical Cox model [R46]. A benchmark of eight early, intermediate and late integration methods for colorectal cancer subtyping identified similarity network fusion (SNF) as the top performer across simulated and real-world datasets [R4]. A separate study benchmarking 20 statistical, machine-learning and deep-learning methods against gold-standard prognostic and therapeutic biomarkers ranked DeePathNet and DeepKEGG as top performers [R50]. The implication is sobering for the deep-learning community: statistical and machine-learning methods (boosting, penalized regression, random forest) implemented with a comparatively small methodological footprint remain competitive with far more elaborate architectures on tabular multi-omics data, and the additional complexity of graph attention, variational autoencoders or cycleGAN-based encoders is rarely justified by accuracy alone on cancer benchmarks.

Several limitations cut across this whole class of tools. First, the abstraction layers—moiraine, miodin, timeOmics—are R-centric, which makes them composable with the Bioconductor infrastructure (MultiAssayExperiment, SummarizedExperiment) but more difficult to weave into Python ecosystems that increasingly dominate deep-learning for omics. Second, the more specialized packages such as MUUMI, CancerSubtypes or the NMF-plus-metaheuristic framework combining adaptive gorilla troops optimization with sparse-joint NMF for cancer subtyping [R43] often lack head-to-head comparisons against the algorithms they are intended to complement, so claims of added value rest on demonstration rather than systematic benchmarking. Third, most frameworks are validated on a small number of case studies (IPF transcriptomes and THP-1 macrophages for MUUMI [R2]; Arabidopsis stress data for mixOmics [R16]; iHMP diabetes for timeOmics [R20]; TCGA glioblastoma and melanoma for the STATegra framework [R24]), which limits generalizability. The narrow evidence base and the absence of matched-condition head-to-head benchmarks across this entire class—including the Bioconductor-based microbiome workflows discussed later—mean that tool choice in practice rests on scope and infrastructure fit rather than demonstrated superiority on any standardized workload.

Microbiome research has long grappled with the gap between taxonomy-oriented surveys and functional understanding of microbial communities. The shift toward host–microbiome multi-omics—where metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, metaproteomics, metabolomics and host-response layers must be jointly analysed—exposes a sobering reality: most tools remain optimised for human cohorts and 16S-derived taxon profiles rather than for the cross-kingdom, functional, and non-model contexts in which microbiomes actually live. Aligning heterogeneous meta-omics layers with host molecular phenotypes remains the central unmet challenge that distinguishes microbiome-centred integration from generic cancer or single-cell pipelines, and the tools that address it remain unevenly distributed across the problems they claim to solve.

EasyMultiProfiler (EMP) is presented as a microbiome-focused workflow built on the SummarizedExperiment and MultiAssayExperiment data structures, organised into five interconnected modules—data extraction, preparation, support, analysis and visualisation—for standardised, reproducible multi-omics microbiome data integration [R1]. The motivation articulated in the EMP paper emphasises inconsistent sample coverage, heterogeneous data formats and complex analytical workflows as bottlenecks that erode reproducibility [R1]. In our reading, EMP's contribution lies in coordinating these steps within a coherent R-based workflow rather than introducing new integration mathematics; whether this coordination actually reduces methodological inconsistency between meta-omics datasets is a claim that would require benchmarking against equivalently curated pipelines and is not demonstrated in the cited work [R1]. The EMP publication does not document performance on non-model host-associated microbiomes, nor does it explicitly address whether the framework natively ingests cross-kingdom meta-omics layers alongside host omics [R1]. Practical dimensions such as explicit compositionality handling, missing-data policy and phylogeny-aware integration are not characterised in the available evidence either. The reader should therefore treat EMP as a documented R/Bioconductor option for host-microbiome multi-omics integration, not as a universal solution for cross-kingdom functional meta-omics.

gNOMO was built precisely for the underserved non-model case, integrating up to three meta-omics levels—metagenomics, metatranscriptomics and metaproteomics—through a Snakemake-managed pipeline demonstrated on the cockroach Blattella germanica gut microbiome [R26]. Its contribution is the explicit acknowledgement that sparse reference annotation is the rule for invertebrate, environmental and engineered microbiome studies, and that reproducibility tooling must therefore be paired with database-aware assembly and quantification [R26]. Whether gNOMO natively incorporates host transcriptomics or metabolomics is not described in the available evidence; this is one practical gap that prospective users should evaluate against their own study designs. The contrast with EMP is therefore one of scope rather than methodological superiority: gNOMO targets raw meta-omics assembly for non-model hosts [R26], while EMP provides reproducible downstream integration on a Bioconductor data-class substrate [R1], and the two together sketch a fuller workflow than either alone.

CFViSA offers a web-based route, providing 79 analysis tools spanning sequence processing, visualisation and statistical analysis, combined with microbiome and transcriptome pipelines behind a unified interface [R40]. This lowers the barrier to entry for groups without dedicated bioinformatics capacity, but the platform is best characterised on current evidence as a statistical and visualisation suite; the upstream processing steps it actually performs are not specified in sufficient detail, so users requiring raw metagenomic read assembly or metapeptide identification should not assume coverage [R40]. As such, CFViSA complements rather than substitutes for dedicated meta-omics engines such as gNOMO's assembly pipeline [R26] or the upstream processing that EMP presupposes [R1].

The conceptual roadmaps proposed in recent reviews highlight precisely where these tools underperform. Perspective work on integrating multi-omics technologies to decipher microbiome functions emphasises standardised workflows, FAIR-compliant data objects, benchmarked datasets and community-driven initiatives as prerequisites for credible functional inference [R54], while translational reviews on inflammatory bowel disease argue that gut-microbiota-centred multi-omics must move beyond taxonomic dysbiosis signatures toward quantitative, longitudinally validated, action-linked biomarkers [R58]. Neither roadmap is operationally realised by the microbiome-centred tools examined here, and the available evidence does not establish whether any of them can recover known host–microbe mechanisms from integrated meta-omics in a head-to-head, community-accepted benchmark.

In sum, the microbiome-centred segment of the integration landscape is characterised by uneven coverage: EMP provides a reproducible Bioconductor workflow for host-microbiome multi-omics integration [R1], gNOMO pioneers non-model meta-omics reproducibility [R26], and CFViSA democratises downstream statistics [R40], but the field still over-relies on 16S-derived taxonomy, lacks a unified engine for functional meta-omics across kingdoms, and has no consensus benchmark for evaluating these workflows. The most consequential limitation across the board is that none of these tools has been benchmarked against the others on a shared, functionally annotated meta-omics testbed, leaving their relative accuracy largely an open question.

The browser-accessible tier of multi-omics software has expanded substantially over the past five years, in part because dedicated web platforms shield end-users from installation burdens, environment management and version drift. The most mature general-purpose example is the Analyst suite, in which ExpressAnalyst and MetaboAnalyst handle per-omics normalisation and univariate statistics, OmicsNet performs knowledge-driven integration through biological networks, and OmicsAnalyst conducts data-driven integration through joint dimensionality reduction; the suite was demonstrated on a human pancreatic islet transcriptomics, proteomics and lipidomics study, and the individual components are described as fully functional standalone resources usable independently [R8]. Comparable breadth is offered by ExpOmics, which combines seven applications and four toolkits exposing 28 customizable analysis functions—including differential expression, co-expression, WGCNA, feature selection and functional enrichment—across genes, mRNAs, lncRNAs, miRNAs, circRNAs, piRNAs and proteins without organism restriction, and which additionally pre-loads 22,427 TCGA transcriptomic datasets for browsing [R41]. A more focused but still general resource is CFViSA, which integrates 79 analysis tools spanning sequence processing, visualisation and statistical analysis for microbiome and transcriptome data behind a unified web interface [R40]. These platforms demonstrate that genuine analytical depth can be achieved without writing code, but they also expose an inherent tension: the same menu that enables rapid exploration simultaneously constrains users to a curated catalogue of methods and parameters.

Single-cell-focused web platforms have proliferated because the algorithmic complexity of scRNA-seq, scATAC-seq, CyTOF and spatial workflows is particularly daunting for non-computational users. The single-cell analyst is illustrative: it supports six single-cell omics types plus spatial transcriptomics, automates QC, processing and phenotype-specific analyses, and exposes over 20 interactive visualisations in both online and offline modes [R6]. The trade-off is that the algorithmic choices—normalisation strategy, dimensionality reduction method, clustering resolution—are baked into the workflow; users receive polished outputs but typically cannot swap in alternative implementations without returning to a command-line tool.

Disease-specific databases represent the most curated end of the spectrum, in which pre-computed cohorts and harmonised annotations substitute for any user-side data processing. CPMOAD uniformly integrates RNA-seq, DNA methylation and curated molecular interaction records for preeclampsia, providing interactive differential expression, methylation and pathway enrichment modules against a preprocessed backbone [R7]. LOSTdb manually curates 295 multi-omics datasets spanning bulk RNA-seq, genomic, proteomic, methylation and scRNA-seq modalities and annotates each sample with both literature-based classical subtypes and NMF-derived meta-program subtypes [R34]. The clear strength of such resources is the elimination of upstream processing decisions and the ability to query across many studies at once. The equally clear weakness is curation drift: reference datasets, gene-model annotations and pathway definitions age quickly, and database-style platforms are vulnerable to becoming stale unless the curators commit to continuous re-ingestion of public data and periodic re-versioning of upstream references. Users should therefore treat pre-computed results as starting points rather than definitive answers.

Pathway- and network-oriented visualisation web servers occupy a more specialised niche. PhenoMultiOmics reconstructs enzymatic-reaction-based multi-omics networks linking genes, proteins and metabolites across cancer types and includes biomarker discovery modules for differential expression and pathway enrichment [R14]. NOODAI constructs joint interaction networks from per-omics representative traits and applies the MONET decomposition tool to identify functionally connected modules in clinical multi-omics datasets [R33]. A complementary network integration framework, MINGLE, fuses multi-omics data into a single graph and was applied to glioma heterogeneity [R31]. These platforms excel at producing publication-ready visualisations but, like other GUI tools, fix the underlying graph-construction algorithms and database versions, so reproducing an identical figure in two years' time may require running a different tool.

Radiogenomics and clinical-translational GUIs illustrate the niche where the ease-of-use case is strongest. MuSA is a Shiny-based tool that wraps the MultiAssayExperiment data structure to combine genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and radiomic features in a single interface for breast cancer radiogenomic studies [R25]. MOPAW is a point-and-click graphical workflow hosted on the Cancer Genomics Cloud that automates preprocessing, dimensionality reduction and MOGSA pathway analysis across copy number, transcriptomic, proteomic and phosphoproteomic data [R18]. The Multi-omics Analysis Sandbox Toolkit further lowers the barrier by integrating clinical data with single- and multi-omics datasets and supporting collaborative sharing of analyses and biomarker candidates [R15]. At the visual periphery, R packages such as chromoMap, which interactively plots genomic and multi-omics features onto chromosomal coordinates [R44], and MultiModalGraphics, which annotates scatterplots and heatmaps with fold-changes, p-values and q-values while interoperating with MultiAssayExperiment, limma, voom and iClusterPlus [R52], occupy a hybrid space between scripted analysis and Shiny-style interactivity, sometimes exposed as widgets within larger web platforms.

For microbiome-centred work the practical question is whether these platforms handle the field's specific data challenges: compositionality, sparsity and phylogenetic structure across heterogeneous meta-omics layers. The available evidence does not address these questions systematically for any single tool. CFViSA's published description [R40] emphasises sequence processing and statistical analysis but does not document explicit compositional data handling, centred log-ratio transforms, or phylogenetic-aware integration; whether CFViSA accepts phylogenetic input cannot be determined from the abstract. Among the programmatic alternatives used in microbiome settings, EMP organises a host-microbiome workflow over Bioconductor containers but the available documentation does not establish compositionality handling, missing-data treatment beyond the general acknowledgement of inconsistent sample coverage, or phylogenetic input support as documented features [R1]. Users should therefore not assume that a given GUI's "multi-omics" label implies microbiome-aware methods; explicit feature checks against each study's data characteristics remain necessary.

The cumulative picture is that web servers and GUI tools have compressed the time from raw data to figure enormously, particularly for clinical and disease-focused communities. Several persistent limitations deserve candid acknowledgement. First, the algorithms are frozen: a new method published last month will not appear until the next platform release, and users cannot easily benchmark alternative implementations [R8, R41]. Second, methodological transparency is reduced because the wrapper code that links a parameter to an underlying R or Python function is rarely visible. Third, customisation is shallow—new statistical tests, alternative normalisations or non-standard covariates are typically not exposed. Fourth, database-style platforms are subject to curation drift and stale reference sets, so that pre-computed results can lag behind the literature by years [R7, R34]. Conversely, programmatic frameworks such as EMP [R1], moiraine [R3] and miodin [R48] trade installation overhead and coupling to Bioconductor release cycles for transparency, extensibility and the ability to swap methods; the appropriate tool choice depends on the user's computational fluency and on whether the question demands confirmatory reproducibility or exploratory hypothesis generation.

The substrate on which analytical tools sit is rarely scrutinised as carefully as the algorithms they run, yet the choice of data structure has profound consequences for downstream reproducibility and interoperability. The MultiAssayExperiment class introduced in the Bioconductor ecosystem provides coordinated representation, storage and operation on multiple diverse genomics datasets and ships ready-to-analyse TCGA multi-omics objects, reducing obstacles to scalable, reproducible analysis [R28]. The same ecosystem supplies the lower-level SummarizedExperiment class, on which most omics-specific Bioconductor packages depend, and together these two containers underpin most modern R-based multi-omics analysis. MultiAssayExperiment has, for instance, been adopted as the integrative data structure for radiogenomic studies in MuSA, where it is wrapped by a Shiny interface to permit interactive exploration of genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and radiomic features within a single coherent object [R25]. The persistence of MultiAssayExperiment across many method implementations illustrates how a container can outlive any single integration algorithm, though the standard is not universal: Python-centred packages such as MUUMI [R2] and BioNeuralNet [R5] maintain their own data representations and do not adopt the Bioconductor container.

Visualisation interoperability is tightly coupled to these containers. chromoMap, an R package for the interactive visualisation of chromosomes, accepts genomic-feature and multi-omics annotations and produces publication-ready plots that integrate across genomic coordinates without imposing a particular upstream analysis pipeline [R44]. MultiModalGraphics similarly exposes annotated scatterplots and heatmaps while interoperating natively with MultiAssayExperiment, limma, voom and iClusterPlus, embedding fold-changes, p-values, q-values and standard deviations directly into the graphical output [R52]. Together these packages demonstrate that the Bioconductor visualisation layer can be added onto the MultiAssayExperiment substrate without forcing users to abandon their preferred differential-abundance or factor-analysis tools. EasyMultiProfiler relies on this same SummarizedExperiment/MultiAssayExperiment substrate, drawing on the same container semantics to deliver the five-module workflow (extraction, preparation, support, analysis and visualisation) [R1].

Outside R, the next layer of reproducibility infrastructure concerns the workflows that wrap these data structures. A particularly instructive example is a multi-omics analysis workflow developed in Nextflow with versioned containers and rich semantic metadata, packaged as a Research Object Crate and shared via WorkflowHub as a FAIR Digital Object; the implementation uses RO-Crate metadata and version control of the workflow and container specification, allowing the entire childhood-externalising-behaviour case study to be re-executed by a third party with minimal effort [R11]. A complementary approach is illustrated by moiraine, an R package for constructing reproducible multi-omics integration pipelines that pre-processes data, runs one or more integration methods and produces standardised visualisations while simplifying comparison across tools [R3]. The two designs embody a real trade-off: the Nextflow/FAIR Digital Object approach prioritises machine-actionable, language-agnostic reuse at the cost of an additional container orchestration layer, whereas the moiraine approach maximises interoperability with existing Bioconductor tooling but ties the workflow to the R execution environment.

Cloud-based approaches add further variation. An interdisciplinary learning module on Google Cloud implements a transcriptomics and epigenetics integration pipeline that guides users through three analytical submodules, providing reproducibility by tying execution to the cloud environment rather than to a portable container definition [R13]. While such modules ease entry for non-computational researchers and standardise pedagogical experiences, their long-term archival value may be more limited than the FAIR Digital Object pattern just described: the platform-specific binding implies that workflows could become inaccessible if the host cloud is re-priced, deprecated or sold. By contrast, the Nextflow-packaged FAIR Digital Object attached to WorkflowHub is designed to remain executable on any infrastructure with a Nextflow runtime and the original container images — a more durable form of reproducibility even when the analysis must be rebuilt on heterogeneous hardware.

It is this infrastructural layer, rather than the algorithmic layer, that most determines whether a published integration method continues to be usable years after publication. Yet methodological benchmarking papers overwhelmingly focus on algorithm selection — including extensive comparative studies in colorectal cancer subtyping [R4], single-cell multi-omics integration [R10] and cancer biomarker discovery [R50] — while giving comparatively little attention to container system, metadata standard or persistent identifier assignment. Empirical evidence on multi-omics reproducibility, while not surveyed exhaustively here, consistently flags unevenness across both R and Python ecosystems: R benefits from Bioconductor's release-cycle discipline, whereas many Python tools are still published without an explicit FAIR-Digital-Object equivalent of RO-Crate and depend on ad hoc container specifications. On this reading, the choice of container substrate is a sound investment in long-term reusability; however, none of the microbiome workflows surveyed here — including EMP — bundles a self-contained FAIR Digital Object alongside its analytical pipeline, so that reproducibility in practice depends on the maturity of the underlying container ecosystem (Bioconductor in R, or individual package maintainers in Python) rather than on a portable, machine-actionable object. Closing that gap represents an open opportunity for the microbial multi-omics community rather than a documented shortcoming of any individual tool.

A growing body of empirical benchmark studies now provides the scaffolding on which claims of "best" integration method rest. For unsupervised molecular subtyping, a recent benchmark of eight early-, intermediate- and late-integration methods on TCGA colorectal cancer data, complemented by simulated multi-omics structures with realistic cross-omic correlations, identified similarity network fusion (SNF) as the top performer across both simulated and real-world settings [R4]. The same study noted that deep-learning alternatives such as DeepMoIC [R12] and MO-GCAN [R29] did not uniformly outperform SNF. MoAGL-SA [R39] is included here for context but was evaluated on BRCA, KIRP and KIRC subtyping rather than the CRC setting, so any cross-method comparison should be read as illustrative rather than head-to-head, and the "specific evaluation axes" to which such methods are confined differ from study to study. This caveat is reinforced by independent benchmarks in cancer survival prediction, where methods that explicitly account for the multi-omics group structure achieved only marginally better predictive accuracy than clinical baselines across 18 TCGA cohorts, with block forest as essentially the only algorithm that significantly outperformed a simple Cox model trained on clinical covariates alone [R46]. The collective message tempers the enthusiasm with which novel deep architectures are often promoted: in clinically meaningful tasks, sophisticated multi-omics models rarely dominate, and gains over carefully tuned clinical predictors are frequently marginal.

The single-cell multi-omics benchmark landscape is more nuanced. A systematic evaluation of 14 protein-abundance/chromatin-accessibility prediction algorithms and 18 multi-omics integration algorithms across 47 single-cell datasets reported that totalVI and scArches dominated protein-imputation tasks, whereas Seurat, MOJITOO and scAI led vertical (same-cell) integration, and totalVI and UINMF were best for horizontal/mosaic integration [R10]. A complementary benchmark of 12 methods on three integration tasks for paired single-cell RNA and ATAC data concluded that different methods have their own advantages on different aspects rather than identifying a universal winner [R37]. These are methodologically honest findings, but they expose a deeper problem: benchmarks that exhaustively catalogue per-method strengths implicitly assume that the practitioner can match task to algorithm, and they do not address whether the best-performing methods in benchmark conditions retain their advantage when applied to new cohorts with different batch structures, cell-type compositions or noise profiles. In short, the benchmarks demonstrate clear leadership in specific niches without resolving whether such leadership generalises beyond the curated training cohorts.

A particularly pointed set of concerns arises from the biomarker-discovery literature. A benchmark of 20 statistical, machine-learning and deep-learning multi-omics biomarker identification methods, evaluated against curated gold-standard prognostic and therapeutic biomarkers across five cancer datasets, found that DeePathNet and DeepKEGG ranked as top performers across both predictive accuracy and biomarker-recovery metrics, and that many high-accuracy deep-learning methods nevertheless failed to recover clinically actionable biomarkers [R50]. The dissociation between accuracy and interpretability is not merely an academic concern: regulators and clinicians require named, mechanistically traceable features, and the benchmark implies that the most accurate black-box models are often the least suitable for translation. Independent reviews of deep learning in tumour genomics have reached a similar conclusion, emphasising the need for explainable AI and federated approaches to bridge the accuracy–translation gap [R56].

Across these benchmarks the field lacks a unified evaluation panel, which makes cross-study comparison hazardous. Different studies use different combinations of silhouette scores, normalised mutual information, the concordance index, area under the precision-recall curve, biomarker overlap with gold standards and stability under resampling. Each metric captures a distinct aspect of method behaviour — clustering compactness, agreement with ground-truth labels, discrimination of censored outcomes, biological plausibility, robustness — and no single score summarises "good integration." A direct consequence is that the same method can rank first by silhouette and tenth by NMI on identical data, with no principled basis for choosing one ordering over the other. Benchmarks also differ in their reliance on synthetic versus real data; simulated cohorts tend to favour the integration strategies whose assumptions they encode, whereas real-world TCGA or single-cell datasets reward robustness to noise and confounders [R4, R46]. Reproducible benchmarking infrastructures — including dedicated pipelines for method comparison such as moiraine [R3], FAIR Digital Object workflows [R11], and emerging microbiome-specific multi-omics standards [R54] — are beginning to address this gap, but the community still has no accepted reference panel analogous to the standardised assays that structured kinase-inhibitor development, and microbiome-specific benchmarks are notably thin on the dimensions that matter for compositional, sparse and phylogenetically structured data. Until such a panel exists, claims that any single method "wins" the integration problem should be read with caution, and the practical recommendation is to interpret benchmark rankings as task-specific evidence rather than as universal endorsements.

The five-criterion rubric that frames this survey — scalability, data structures, interoperability, documentation, maintenance and reproducibility — is not applied tool-by-tool in the foregoing pages because the underlying evidence is unevenly distributed: some tools ship version-controlled releases and container images, others are documented only through web interfaces or method papers, and very few have been independently benchmarked against matched competitors. We treat this rubric as a checklist for downstream readers rather than a scored instrument, and we flag longitudinal-cohort and microbiome benchmarks as the most conspicuous empirical gaps that the field should close before comparative claims can be grounded in shared evaluation.

EasyMultiProfiler (EMP) is positioned in this review as one R-based microbiome workflow that anchors the analysis life-cycle on the Bioconductor container ecosystem [R1]. Its architecture organizes the workflow into five interconnected modules — data extraction, preparation, support, analysis and visualization — built directly on SummarizedExperiment and MultiAssayExperiment, the coordinated classes that have become a widely used substrate for multi-assay handling in R [R1, R28]. In framing EMP this way, we treat the workflow as a structured wrapper that allows users to assemble microbiome cohorts and dispatch them to established analytical methods without having to reconcile file formats ad hoc [R1]. The EMP authors motivate the work in terms of inconsistent sample coverage, heterogeneous data formats and complex analytical workflows that erode reproducibility in microbiome multi-omics — a field-level diagnosis the tools reviewed here share, and one that EMP treats as the principal engineering bottleneck rather than as an open methodological problem [R1].

The Bioconductor anchoring has clear practical consequences across the dimensions considered in this review. Through the coordinated representation, subsetting semantics and interoperability documented for MultiAssayExperiment [R28], EMP interoperates with the broader R/Bioconductor ecosystem that consumes these classes, supporting reuse of existing differential-expression, clustering and visualization utilities. Documentation, version-controlled release and maintenance follow Bioconductor conventions. The alternative packaging strategy documented by Niehues et al. [R11] — a Nextflow-based workflow with containers, version control and rich semantic metadata, packaged as a Research Object Crate and shared via WorkflowHub as a FAIR Digital Object — illustrates a contrasting approach: self-contained archival packaging with rich semantic description, but at the cost of integration with the Bioconductor substrate. Compared with general-purpose R integration packages, the design bet differs. moiraine preprocesses data, runs one or more integration methods, produces visualizations and enables comparison of results across different integration tools, with its strength being comparability across methods rather than microbiome specificity [R3]. miodin provides a workflow-based syntax for vertical and horizontal integration across transcriptomic, genomic and proteomic assays with transparent pipelines [R48]. timeOmics contributes dedicated longitudinal modelling and clustering for time-resolved multi-omics, demonstrated on integrative Human Microbiome Project data [R20]. EMP does not attempt to subsume these contributions; it offers a microbiome-oriented orchestration layer that, in the absence of a head-to-head benchmark, trades breadth of mathematical machinery for cohort-level reproducibility within a single Bioconductor substrate [R1].

The most informative microbiome-specific comparison is with gNOMO, a Snakemake-based pipeline for integrated metagenomics, metatranscriptomics and metaproteomics from non-model organisms [R26]. gNOMO excels at the upstream, sequence-derived layers and at reproducible workflow management on non-model systems but requires manual cross-kingdom host-microbe alignment [R26]. EMP's emphasis is complementary: it sits downstream, taking already-processed microbiome features and integrating them with host omics within a single MultiAssayExperiment container [R1]. On the available evidence, EMP and gNOMO address different points along the methodological axis — upstream meta-omics assembly in non-model systems versus downstream host-microbe integration — and neither subsumes the other.

Versus graphical platforms, the trade-offs cut in both directions. MuSA wraps MultiAssayExperiment in a Shiny-based graphical interface aimed at radiogenomic studies, adding imaging-derived features [R25]; the Analyst suite combines ExpressAnalyst, MetaboAnalyst, OmicsNet and OmicsAnalyst into a code-free environment for single-omics analysis, knowledge-driven network integration and data-driven joint dimensionality reduction [R8]. These platforms lower the entry barrier for non-computational users and provide interactive visualization, but they typically require data upload to external servers, constrain users to the analyses pre-implemented in the web backend, and offer limited algorithmic transparency. EMP retains the transparency and extensibility of a scriptable R workflow with version-controlled dependencies and local execution, but it requires Bioconductor proficiency that GUI tools do not, and its analytical scope is paced by the same Bioconductor release cadence that constrains other ecosystem packages such as mixOmics [R27], MultiAssayExperiment itself [R28], miodin [R48] and CancerSubtypes [R49]. Users without substantial R expertise will therefore find the GUI platforms more accessible, whereas experienced R users gain methodological transparency and local reproducibility through EMP and its Bioconductor peers.

The critical assessment must be candid. EMP's contribution is the standardized five-module wrapper around an established data-class ecosystem, not novel integration mathematics; methodological novelty relative to DIABLO within mixOmics [R27], MOFA-based factor analysis (as extended by MOTL [R32]), similarity-network fusion [R4] or the deep-learning integrators [R5, R12] is modest. The accompanying limitations follow from the same design choice. First, the available evidence does not establish that EMP outperforms any specific integration algorithm under matched conditions; the benchmark studies surveyed here [R4, R10, R37, R46, R50] do not include EMP, so claims of competitive performance are unsupported. Second, although EMP is framed for host-microbiome integration [R1] and on this basis is plausibly well suited to human and mammalian microbiome projects with established reference databases, its demonstrated scope does not include raw meta-omics assembly upstream of feature tables for non-model systems; users with that requirement should evaluate gNOMO [R26] in parallel. Third, EMP is not aimed at single-cell multi-omics integration, where dedicated benchmarking identified different top performers (totalVI, scArches, Seurat, MOJITOO, scAI) [R10], nor at radiomic or imaging-augmented integration, where MuSA has an established scope [R25]. Fourth, reproducibility depends on the maturity of its dependent Bioconductor packages rather than on a self-contained FAIR Digital Object workflow of the kind described by Niehues et al. [R11], which documents Nextflow execution, containerised components and rich semantic metadata for archival reuse, in contrast to EMP's ecosystem-integrated but externally versioned dependencies. What the underlying evidence does support is that, for the host-microbiome use case, a coherent class-coordinated wrapper can lower the engineering overhead of column-metadata harmonisation, feature-ID reconciliation and reproducible analysis assembly — a workflow-level contribution rather than a methodological one.

A central controversy in current multi-omics methodology is whether the proliferation of deep learning architectures delivers meaningful advances over classical statistical frameworks, or whether it represents incremental architectural variation over a common encoder–decoder template. Trustworthiness-focused proposals such as TMODINET illustrate the field's stated ambitions: combining self-attention, graph convolutional components and Dirichlet-based uncertainty estimation to address calibration and interpretability in cancer diagnostics [R9]. The appeal of calibrated, interpretable predictions in high-stakes clinical settings is obvious, yet many recent methods pair attention with graph convolutional networks in essentially interchangeable configurations, and their claimed gains over supervised regularised regression are often within the noise envelope seen in independent benchmarking [R9, R46, R50]. Large survival-prediction benchmarks across TCGA datasets have repeatedly shown that methods explicitly modelling multi-omics group structure offer only marginal improvements, with only block forest outperforming a clinical Cox model decisively across most cancer types [R46]. In cancer biomarker discovery, deep architectures identified as top performers in one benchmark often fail to generalise to external cohorts [R50]. The community should therefore treat self-attention plus graph-convolutional combinations with scepticism when external validation, calibration curves and decision-curve analyses are absent; the burden of proof for clinical translation has not shifted simply because the encoder backbone has become more elaborate. It should also be acknowledged that none of TMODINET, the survival-prediction cohort and the biomarker benchmark use matched data, so direct head-to-head claims across these studies rest on inference rather than on a common reference.

A second frontier concerns resolution. Single-cell multi-omics has moved rapidly from co-profiled RNA and chromatin accessibility towards single-molecule, barcode-indexed assays that also capture spatial localisation [R19, R51]. Pipelines such as ScSmOP illustrate that the bottleneck has shifted from chemistry to the engineering of barcode identification, mapping and reproducible deconvolution for ligation-based and synthesis-based assays [R19]. At the same time, single-cell graph attention methods continue to emerge with limited head-to-head comparison [R51], and benchmarking across 47 single-cell datasets suggests that the practical choice of integration method is still highly task-dependent, with no dominant approach across vertical, horizontal and mosaic integration regimes [R10]. The availability of well-curated evaluation resources and modular single-cell platforms will determine whether the next generation of methods is judged by architectural novelty or by measurable improvements on externally validated tasks [R6, R37].

Beyond cellular resolution, the integration question itself is being redefined. Isoform-level integration recognises that alternative splicing can assign distinct functions to transcripts of the same gene, yet current pipelines rarely exploit isoform–isoform interactions or integrate heterogeneous feature domains convincingly [R36]. Frameworks such as CrossIsoFun attempt to address this with omics-specific graph convolutional encoders, view-correlation discovery and cycleGAN-based feature harmonisation, but the evaluation remains largely retrospective and confined to bulk omics [R36]. Complementary efforts push integration into three-dimensional chromatin space, using topologically associating domains as biologically motivated anchors that respect the genome's regulatory architecture [R23]. InterTADs demonstrates the value of this approach in chronic lymphocytic leukemia, where confining integration to TADs yields reproducible differences between normal and malignant cells and biologically interpretable enrichments [R23]. The trajectory from gene-level to isoform-level to TAD-level integration suggests that biological scale, rather than algorithmic sophistication, will be the principal driver of insight, particularly when coupled with targeted TF–target discovery pipelines that use ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq and RNA-seq in concert [R45, R47].

Network-based approaches are simultaneously gaining traction as an alternative to embedding-centric deep learning. Random-walk with restart on multilayer heterogeneous networks, exemplified by multiXrank in the COVID-19 setting, propagates signal across omics-derived features and curated knowledge graphs to identify biosignatures associated with specific disease phases [R38]. This family of methods offers mechanistic interpretability that attention-based encoders often lack, but their results depend heavily on the completeness and bias of the underlying knowledge graphs and on how missing edges are penalised. Hybrid platforms that fuse variable selection with graph integration, such as MINGLE for glioma heterogeneity, are beginning to address this [R31], but the field still lacks principled criteria for deciding when a multilayer random walk is preferable to a well-tuned matrix factorisation or a similarity-network fusion approach [R4].

Spatially resolved and clinically integrative applications are emerging as the most ambitious proving grounds. Reviews of immunometabolic heterogeneity at the lung cancer tumour-immune interface synthesise single-cell transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics and spatial profiling into resistance-linked metabolic subtypes, but stop short of providing tool-grade infrastructure for reproducible re-analysis [R60]. Habitat radiomics extends conventional radiomics by using AI to define intratumoral subregions whose molecular correlates can, in principle, be mapped to omics profiles [R59]. Likewise, recurrent pregnancy loss research now invokes multi-omics stratification across immunity, microbiome and metabolism, yet existing computational toolkits for these data are mostly borrowed from oncology or generic single-cell workflows [R53]. The conceptual appeal of these syntheses is high; their translational readiness is low, and what the published data do not yet demonstrate is robust, prospective validation of any of the proposed subtyping schemes.

Exosome-based biomarker discovery for cardiovascular disease exemplifies the translational gap most starkly. AI approaches ranging from Random Forest ensembles to graph neural networks integrate EV-derived multi-omics with clinical metadata, with reported AUCs typically between 0.80 and 0.92, yet reproducibility is undermined by non-standardised isolation, pre-analytic variability and small discovery cohorts [R55]. Similar concerns apply to neoantigen pipelines that integrate WGS, transcriptomics and proteomics with convolutional predictors, where portability and external validation remain unresolved despite promising internal performance [R35]. Across these domains, integration platforms often propagate batch effects unless explicit harmonisation, ComBat-style adjustment or domain-adversarial training is applied, and the absence of such steps is rarely reported transparently.

The reproducibility crisis is therefore not a peripheral concern but the central axis around which the field's emerging frontiers must be evaluated. FAIR-packaged, containerised workflows distributed as Research Object Crates offer one route, but adoption outside demonstration case studies remains limited [R11]. Reviews of microbiome multi-omics explicitly call for benchmarked datasets, community-driven standards and harmonised reporting before the next wave of methods can be fairly compared [R54]. Closing this gap will require not only better containers and metadata but also structural incentives that reward external validation; without a shared benchmark infrastructure in which tools such as MOFA, DIABLO, EMP and the deep-learning family are evaluated on matched host-microbiome data, tool choice will continue to rest on scope and infrastructure fit rather than demonstrated superiority.

Practical guidance must be calibrated to the user. Bench biologists and clinical microbiologists seeking entry points into multi-omics analysis typically benefit most from web- or GUI-based platforms that bundle preprocessing, statistical testing and visualisation behind an interactive interface and require minimal local installation [R8, R40, R41]. Computational microbiologists already working in R/Bioconductor may prefer an opinionated workflow that builds on shared container classes rather than assembling bespoke scripts; EMP provides one such option, organised as a five-module (extraction, preparation, support, analysis, visualisation) framework on SummarizedExperiment and MultiAssayExperiment [R1], while moiraine and miodin offer complementary R/Bioconductor entry points with different scope [R3, R48]. For studies combining metagenomics, metatranscriptomics and metabolomics in moderate-sized cohorts, the choice between these R-based workflows should be guided by data modality and engineering overhead in the user's own ecosystem, not by claims of demonstrated superiority, since head-to-head benchmarking under matched host-microbiome conditions has not, to our knowledge, been published. Biostatisticians and method-oriented researchers will usually want lower-level access: the MultiAssayExperiment Bioconductor class and its ready-to-analyse TCGA objects remain the most mature substrate for bespoke modelling [R28], and reproducible pipeline orchestrators such as moiraine enable systematic comparison of integration methods [R3]. Computational method developers should treat standardised containers and FAIR packaging as table stakes, since the marginal value of yet another clustering or matrix-factorisation algorithm is rapidly approaching zero without rigorous evaluation against shared benchmark panels [R50]. Clinicians and translational scientists face a different trade-off: in contexts such as inflammatory bowel disease or recurrent pregnancy loss, decision support demands not only multi-omics signatures but also analytical validity, external validation, calibration and action-linked thresholds before any pipeline can be deployed at the bedside [R53, R58].

A short-term roadmap follows directly from the surveyed limitations. First, harmonised data structures — extending the MultiAssayExperiment paradigm into longitudinal, single-cell and microbiome-specific contexts — are the most consequential investment; timeOmics already demonstrates that this framework can be enriched for repeated-measures designs without abandoning interoperability [R20, R28], and microbiome-centred tools should explicitly address compositionality, sparsity, phylogeny-aware integration and partial-coverage sample handling as design constraints rather than afterthoughts. Second, FAIR packaging of workflows must become routine: packaging pipelines as FAIR Digital Objects with rich semantic metadata, as illustrated by Nextflow-based case studies, ensures that humans and machines can discover, cite and reuse computational artefacts, and the microbiome community should adopt this convention proactively [R11]. Third, the field needs shared benchmark panels grounded in clinically meaningful endpoints; systematic evaluations of biomarker discovery, clustering and survival prediction show that top performers depend strongly on data modality, sample size and biological question, and consensus panels are essential for fair comparison [R4, R46, R50]. Fourth, the broader roadmap for standardised microbiome workflows [R54] remains largely a set of recommendations rather than operationalised tooling; whether EMP, moiraine, miodin and the GUI/web tools discussed here collectively address compositionality, sparsity, phylogeny and host-microbiome coupling in a comparable way has not been assessed, on the evidence surveyed here, against a common rubric. Fifth, deep learning methods remain hampered by opaque confidence; uncertainty-aware architectures that quantify predictive variance, such as the Dirichlet-based estimation used in TMODINET, should be adopted as a quality requirement rather than a research luxury [R9].

EMP can be situated within this roadmap as one documented workflow-level option for host-microbiome research, alongside comparable R/Bioconductor substrates such as moiraine and miodin; its five-module organisation over established container classes is consistent with the harmonisation priorities above, and the EMP publication positions reproducibility as its central aim [R1]. Like any single workflow, however, EMP is not a substitute for dedicated single-cell multi-omics frameworks that excel at vertical integration of RNA, protein and chromatin modalities [R10], nor for spatial-aware platforms linking imaging habitats with molecular profiles [R59], nor for clinical-grade decision-support systems that require regulatory-grade validation, harmonised metadata and prospective calibration [R58]; the EMP paper does not claim coverage of these domains, and the evidence surveyed here does not show that microbiome workflows have yet been stress-tested at clinical-decision scale. Tool choice should be driven by data modality, cohort size, reproducibility constraints and translational stakes, and the coming years will reward contributors who invest in shared infrastructure — containers, benchmarks, semantic metadata and uncertainty quantification — over those who publish isolated algorithms. Realising this potential will require a coordinated commitment to those foundations if multi-omics is to become a routinely reliable component of biomedical research rather than remain a methodological showcase.
